summary.title: Video Game Physics Tutorial - Part I: An Introduction to Rigid Body Dynamics
summary.one_liner: You learn how rigid body motion works in game physics engines, from particle simulation with semi-implicit Euler integration to 2D rigid bodies with mass, center of mass, moment of inertia and torque, with C code examples.
keywords: how do physics engines simulate objects
box2d bullet chipmunk jolt rapier physx
takeaways: Rigid bodies are solids that do not deform; their position is the center of mass and their motion is updated each simulation step.
Particle simulation with semi-implicit Euler integration is the stepping stone to rigid body simulation, shown with C code.
Torque from off-center forces changes angular velocity, scaled by the moment of inertia (a box has I = m(w² + h²)/12).
In 2D, a rigid body needs only one scalar for orientation, while 3D requires quaternions and an inertia tensor.
Collisions and constraints are covered in Parts II and III of the series.
summary.summary: This Toptal tutorial, the first of a three-part series by Nilson Souto, introduces rigid body dynamics for game developers. It explains Newton's three laws, the role of a physics engine as a stepped numerical simulation, and the semi-implicit Euler method used by most engines. It then builds up from a C particle simulation to a 2D rigid body simulation covering center of mass, moment of inertia, and torque. The article notes that the simulation is unconstrained (no collisions), leaving collision detection and constraints to later parts, and briefly mentions 3D quaternions and ECS-based engines.
